column2: When Hu Xueyan met the Seventh Lady, both felt as though a lifetime had passed. Looking at one another, they could not keep back their tears. In a month apart, each had acquired many more white hairs. Neither had thought much of their own; only on seeing the other did they understand how worry could ravage a person. Hu, above all, felt like weeping aloud at the thought that the Seventh Lady, already ill herself, had been so distressed on his account. Whenever they met, her first inquiry was usually after Old Madam Hu. This time alone she made an exception, afraid that the question would touch his deepest sorrow. But she could not avoid asking about Madam Luosi. “And Sister Luo? She must have aged a great deal too.” “Indeed she has! I depend on her now.” Hu went on to describe many instances of the warmth and coldness of human relations. The Seventh Lady’s eyes were red, and tears kept gathering. “Rest a little,” Ruixiang interrupted from time to time, hoping to stop these distressing conversations. At last she could bear it no longer. “It is time for your medicine and sleep,” she ordered. “Yes, yes!” Hu felt guilty. “Rest properly, Seventh Sister, and do not worry. With Yingchun helping me, I shall certainly get through.” Gu accompanied him downstairs. They had just settled in the study when a servant brought a visitor’s card: Shen Lansheng, a shift supervisor in the telegraph bureau’s decoding room. “Probably a reply from Hangzhou,” Gu said, handing Hu the card. “He is a good friend. Would you like to meet him?” “No. I had better stay out of sight.” “Very well.” Gu went to receive him in the drawing room.

Only a wall separated the drawing room from the study, and the door stood open, so Hu could hear their conversation clearly. “There are two telegrams concerning Circuit Intendant Hu. I made copies specially and brought them over.” The unfamiliar voice must be Shen’s. Silence followed. Unable to restrain himself, Hu peered through the gap in the door. Gu was reading the messages. “I am deeply obliged,” he said when he had finished. “If there is any further news, please let me know immediately, day or night. I shall tell Intendant Hu of your help. He will certainly show his gratitude.” “There is no question of that. I merely feel he has been unjustly treated. If I can do a little to help, it will satisfy my conscience.” “Yes, indeed. He may be coming to Shanghai in the next day or two. I shall arrange for you to meet him then.” “Very good. I shall take my leave.” After seeing his visitor out, Gu returned to the study with an unusually grave expression. Plainly the two telegrams contained bad news. “Yingchun,” Hu asked calmly, “what do they say?” “Something entirely unexpected.” Gu handed him the copies.

They contained two imperial decrees telegraphed by the Shenbao’s Beijing correspondent. The first began by citing the report of Zhou Jiamei, prefect of Shuntian, and Left Censor-in-Chief Bi Daoyuan, the senior official supervising the prefecture. Ordered to investigate the Fukangfu deposits of Assistant Grand Secretary and Minister of Punishments Wenyu, they had discovered a deposit of 460,000 taels. Of this, 100,000 belonged to Wenhui, formerly provincial treasurer of Jiangxi, who said he had entrusted Wenyu with depositing it for him. The remaining 360,000 appeared in the books merely under “Wen Household”; whether it belonged to Wenyu could not be determined. In such cases the usual instruction was to “order Wenyu to submit a clear explanation.” His answer had been frank enough. During the past twenty years he had received numerous revenue appointments; since his transfer from Fujian to the capital, he had repeatedly served as superintendent of the Chongwen Gate customs. His accumulated official pay and allowances, together with habitual economy, accounted for the 360,000 taels deposited at Fukangfu. The decree accepted his explanation as “substantially truthful,” but considered the amount “somewhat large” and ordered him to contribute 100,000 taels for public use. Shuntian prefecture was to withdraw the money from Fukangfu and remit it to the Ministry of Revenue. “Yingchun,” Hu said after reading this message, “contact our Beijing branch. Those hundred thousand taels must be assembled immediately. Better to send them to the Ministry ourselves before Shuntian presses us.” “I think this should be dealt with as part of the general liquidation,” Gu objected. “Perhaps we can wait and see.” “No. Not a single coin can be withheld. Better to pay early than late.” “Very well. I shall do as you wish. But read the second telegram first.”

Hu’s expression changed when he read it, though he quickly recovered. “This gives Lord Zuo a difficult problem.” After a moment he asked, “He will have received the court dispatch already, I suppose?” “Of course.” “And here? Once it appears in tomorrow’s Shenbao, everyone will know.” “Not tomorrow. It will not appear until the day after.” Hu remained silent for some time, his lips firmly closed. “We cannot hide this from Seventh Sister.” “No.” Gu paused. “She said she feared it would come to this.” “She said that?” “Yes.” Gu could give the exact date. “Four days ago.” “Good!” Hu rose abruptly. “If she could foresee this, she must have been considering what I ought to do. Four days will have given her time to think it through. Let us consult her.” Gu accompanied him upstairs again. Hearing their steps, Ruixiang came softly out and held two fingers to her lips. “She has just fallen asleep.” Before Gu could answer, Hu tugged at his clothes and began quietly descending the stairs. Back in the study, he seemed to have formed a plan; his manner was no longer hesitant. “Go and speak to Shen Lansheng for me. You decide how we should thank him. Above all, ask him not to spread the news.” “I told him that already.” “Better to impress it on him again. And call at Jixian Lane on the way. Tell Old Mi that I am staying here. While Seventh Sister rests, I shall think everything over. By the time you return she should be awake, and we can discuss it together.”

There were only three people in the bedroom; even Ruixiang was excluded. The Seventh Lady had indeed prepared herself for the news. When Hu handed her the telegram, she asked calmly, “Has it come from Beijing?” “It is an imperial decree sent through the Grand Council,” Gu answered. “You predicted correctly.” “Then I have become a crow croaking misfortune.” Turning to her husband, she said, “A decree is no songbook in seven-character lines. I cannot even tell where its sentences end, and there will be characters I do not know. Read it to me.” Gu read slowly: “Fukang has now closed, owing very large sums in public funds and deposits from many quarters. Its proprietor, Hu Guangyong, expectant circuit intendant for Jiangxi, is hereby dismissed from office forthwith. Zuo Zongtang is ordered to have him brought before him for rigorous investigation and compel him promptly to settle, one by one, the public and private liabilities outstanding in various places. Should he dare delay full payment, he is to be severely punished without further ado. It is also reported that Hu Guangyong owns more than twenty pawnshops in various provinces, as well as quantities of cocoons and silk worth several million taels stored in Zhejiang. The governor-general is to communicate officially with the governors-general and governors concerned, directing them to investigate and deal with each item. Let him be informed of this decree.” Gu looked up. “Did you understand?” “How could I not?” The Seventh Lady raised her eyes. “Little Uncle, congratulations! It is much better than I expected.” Hu stared; Gu too found this startling. “What is there to congratulate him on?” “The court has entrusted Little Uncle’s case to Lord Zuo. Is that not one reason? Someone is helping him.” Hu understood first. “How clearly an onlooker sees! If someone has helped, it must be Grand Secretary Wen. He is related to Prince Gong.”

“Yes, yes.” Gu turned to his wife. “You say it is much better than you expected. What had you expected?” “It is past now. There is no need to say.” “No,” Hu replied firmly. “We have reached this point and must discuss everything thoroughly. You need not spare my feelings.” “I thought that, besides dismissal, there would be confiscation. Now Lord Zuo is merely to ‘investigate rigorously.’ Nor is the command to pay everything off outright, but to arrange the settlement. Then it tells him to send official communications to the provincial authorities for investigation and action. As I read it, Governor Liu in Zhejiang must follow Lord Zuo’s instructions: investigate if told to, refrain if not. That makes an enormous difference.” Once she explained, Hu saw the significance. Zhejiang’s governor, Liu Bingzhang, currently bore full responsibility for the liquidation. Although his career was associated with the Huai Army, he was also a Hanlin scholar and did not wish to attach himself to Li Hongzhang. Nevertheless, his deep Huai Army connections made him indirectly susceptible to Li’s influence. Li regarded Hu as one of Zuo’s supporting wings, which must be clipped. To expect Liu to offer special assistance was therefore like climbing a tree to catch fish. Now the court had entrusted settlement of Fukang’s public and private debts to Zuo, who could direct Dexin himself. This was naturally much more favourable to Hu. “Seventh Sister, one word from you has awakened a dreamer. Tell us what to do. You are our female Zhuge Liang; give your orders.” “Do not say that, Little Uncle. I shall suggest a few things for us to discuss. First, telegraph Treasurer De so that he understands the position. Governor Liu no longer has so much control.” “Exactly. That telegram must go at once.”

“We must also contact Lord Zuo without delay,” the Seventh Lady continued. “Will you go yourself, Little Uncle, or have Yingchun explain everything in person?” “I had better go,” Gu volunteered. “It would be inconvenient for Little Uncle now that he has lost his official cap.” This was precisely what Hu wanted. A man dismissed by imperial decree could wear only ordinary clothes. That would not matter to Zuo, but Jiangning contained more expectant circuit intendants than anywhere else in the country. People joked that “thieves were thick as hairs,” playing on the shared sound of dao, their rank and the word for thief. Once the lamps were lit, around the examination compound and the Qinhuai river houses in the south of the city, everyone one met was addressed as “Intendant So-and-so.” They would naturally continue to address Hu in the same way. He would not know whether to accept it silently or explain that he was now a commoner. He was only too glad to avoid such embarrassment. “Yes, Yingchun, please undertake the journey. As a third party, you can speak to Lord Zuo more freely.” “Very well. I shall leave first thing tomorrow. What else should I tell him?” “Convey De Xiaofeng’s particular respects. He is very eager to establish a connection with Lord Zuo. Another supporter among the provincial leaders would be useful to His Excellency too.” Gu knew how keen Dexin was to become a governor. If he could speak for him and obtain Zuo’s promise of a recommendation for advancement, Dexin would naturally work still harder on Hu’s behalf.

“But Treasurer De’s reply will arrive tomorrow if not today,” Gu said. “It may be unwise to lose contact with the foreign buyers. Selling the silk is, after all, our most important business.” “The position is different now,” Hu replied. “Lord Zuo is responsible for the settlement. Whether the silk may be sold is for him to decide. That is why it is best for you to go to Jiangning: you can discuss it with him in person.” “Even if the treasurer’s reply says we may sell?” “We must still follow Lord Zuo’s wishes.” The Seventh Lady could not keep silent. “That is no way to conduct business. The foreigners are what matters now. If you cannot agree on a price, there is nothing to discuss. But if you agree and then cannot sell because you must seek Lord Zuo’s instructions, the delay may make them change their minds.” “You are right.” Hu immediately decided. “The silk must be sold. It is only a question of the price and allowing a few more days. Yingchun, secure the buyer tomorrow morning. Tell him the transaction will certainly go through, and ask him to wait a few days. Foreigners understand by now that patience is necessary whenever officials are involved. If he refuses to wait even a few days, he cannot be sincere, and there is nothing to regret in abandoning such a customer.” “Very well. I shall call on him first thing and set out as soon as I return.” Gu suddenly noticed something. “Why has Old Mi still not come?”

On his way to Shen Lansheng, Gu had followed Hu’s instructions and first called at Jixian Lane. Although Fukang was closed, Mi Benchang and a few clerks remained there. On hearing that Hu had arrived, Mi had immediately said he would come to Gu’s house to “meet Mr Hu.” Nearly three hours had passed since then. Why was there still no sign of him? “An ugly daughter-in-law must meet her parents-in-law eventually. He will come,” the Seventh Lady said. “Little Uncle, have supper while we wait. I wonder whether it is ready.” “It has been ready for some time,” Ruixiang called from the outer sitting room. She entered the bedroom and wheeled the Seventh Lady out. Supper was still elaborate, with many of Hu’s favourite dishes. In the bitter weather there was naturally a hotpot, made with the wine-lees broth of zaobotou, fish balls, sea cucumber, winter bamboo shoots, and the Shandong cabbage known as jiaocai. It reminded Hu of Laotonghe. “Yingchun, did you see A’cai?” “Yes.” “Who is A’cai?” the Seventh Lady asked. “That sounds like a woman’s name.” Hu and Gu exchanged a smile. The news from Beijing had, paradoxically, steadied Hu’s spirits, and Gu felt there was no harm in recounting this unexpected romantic episode. “If Little Uncle had met A’cai just once more in those days, he might now be the proprietor of Laotonghe.” Beginning with that joke, he told the story from the previous night’s meal to his conversation with A’cai that morning. Hu added details from time to time. Stretching over more than twenty years, it was almost a legend. The Seventh Lady and Ruixiang listened with fascination. Hu too learned much that he had never known or even imagined. A’cai’s enduring affection particularly surprised him. He tried hard to recall her appearance then, but could summon only a faint, almost formless image. All he remembered clearly was a slender figure and a pair of large eyes. Supper did not end until midnight. Mi never appeared. “Never mind,” Hu said. “We shall deal with it tomorrow. Sleep comes first.”

Hu slept badly. The chief reason was a newly installed boiler in Gu’s house, which carried steam through lead pipes to the rooms. This Western novelty was known in Shanghai as hot-water heating. Elaborate though Hu’s Yuanbao Street residence was, it had nothing of the kind. The room might be “as warm as spring,” but he was unused to it. Under a silk-floss quilt he woke sweating several times, until he had to get up and find two woollen blankets in a cupboard. Only then did he sleep soundly. When he woke, sunlight filled the windows. Hearing him stir, Ruixiang came to attend to his washing. Naturally she asked after the Hu household, but he answered only, “Everyone is well,” and showed no wish to discuss it. She tactfully let the subject drop. Upstairs, breakfast was waiting with the Seventh Lady, including the customary bowl of bird’s-nest porridge. “Thank you, Seventh Sister. You have it.” “Why will you not eat it? Do not treat yourself badly, Little Uncle.” “It is not that. I have enjoyed more good fortune than I deserved. Now I feel I should treasure what I have.” Before she could answer, hurried footsteps sounded on the stairs, as though someone were running up. Everyone looked. It was Gu. “Little Uncle—Old Mi is dead!” “Dead? Was it a stroke?” “No. He took his own life with opium,” Gu said dejectedly. “He probably swallowed a few pellets after I left. This morning he did not open his door. A’zhang knocked without getting an answer, climbed through the window, and found his body already stiff.” A’zhang was a Fukang clerk. “Why?” Hu shook his head. “There was no need for that.”

“You are truly kindhearted,” the Seventh Lady said. “He always felt the disaster was entirely his doing and could not face you. He came here twice. Whenever he spoke of it, he sighed and blamed himself for going to Ningbo. At that time...” She abruptly stopped. “Go on, Seventh Sister,” Hu urged. Instead of answering, she asked her husband, “How do you know he swallowed the opium as soon as you left?” “They told me that after I went, he shut his door and went to bed. It was only eight o’clock; everyone else was still up.” “Did nobody wonder why he was going to bed so early?” “They did, but no one asked him. A’zhang told me he wondered why Mi was sleeping after saying he would go to see Mr Hu. He meant to look in, but he had arranged to see the evening opera with friends. A featured item was Yang Yuelou’s Eight Great Hammers with the Storytelling Scene, and he was afraid of being late, so he hurried off. After the performance they had supper, and he went straight to bed on returning. Only when he knocked this morning did he discover what had happened.” The Seventh Lady fell silent, though her expression clearly showed she had another interpretation. “There were still several people at Fukang,” Hu said. “Did not one of them notice? Opium is different from hanging. A man would make some sound before dying. Did nobody hear?” “I asked the same thing. Some said they fell asleep as soon as they lay down and heard nothing. Others had gone out strolling and knew nothing about it.” “Then it was fate.” The Seventh Lady could no longer restrain herself. “I do not mean to speak cruelly of the dead, but I think a pretence became reality.” “You mean he only pretended to try to die?” Gu asked. “You know he carried four opium pellets in that translucent horn box. He showed it to people more than once.” “Oh?” Hu listened closely. “Had he been thinking of suicide for some time?”

“Yes.” She looked at Gu. “I do not know whether he told you, but he told me.” “What did he say?” Hu asked. “‘I have wronged Mr Hu terribly. I can repay him only with my life.’” “Did you not tell him to abandon such thoughts?” “Of course I did. I said that men in old stories had sacrificed their lives to save their masters, but the sacrifice had to serve a purpose. Throwing away his life uselessly would do Mr Hu no good.” “And what did he answer?” “He said, ‘Unless I do that, I cannot face what I have done to him.’ But if that was truly his intention, he should have done it long ago. Why wait until he had to meet you? I think he simply had nothing he could say and resorted to making a show of suffering. Someone genuinely determined to die would be concerned above all not to fail. He would choose the place and the means so that he would not easily be discovered; once discovered, he might be saved. Surely the Fukang clerks had seen the pellets he carried. Would they not think of them? Having said he was coming to see you, he suddenly shut himself in and went to bed. Naturally he expected people to grow suspicious and rescue him. After that, however great his wrongdoing, they would forgive him, and he would be spared all the effort of explaining and apologising. Who could have foreseen that nobody would notice? They went to the theatre, strolled about, or went to sleep—things he had never counted on. Little Uncle, you need not grieve too much. By dying, he has escaped having to repay his debts in another life. That is something in his favour too.” “Dead and done with; death ends everything,” Hu said. “But someone must arrange his funeral. Yingchun, I know he did not treat you very well. Still, you were friends. You cannot leave it unattended.”

“Of course. I have already told the Fukang clerks to buy a coffin. I shall spend today settling his affairs and leave tomorrow. Should we telegraph Lord Zuo first?” “Yes.” Gu drafted a message in Hu’s name: “I have just received news from the capital and learned of the severe imperial censure. I am returning to Hangzhou to await orders. Upon receiving a telegraphed command, I shall come in person. Meanwhile, I am sending Mr Gu Yingchun to Jiangning to report everything.” Hu possessed a codebook Zuo had given him. But to show that he was acting openly and obeying the decree in every respect, he expressly instructed Gu to send this message in plain code. “And the foreign buyer?” he asked. “Is everything arranged?” “Good,” Hu continued, turning to the Seventh Lady. “Do you think I should leave today?” “Must you hurry so much?” “Mi’s suicide has made me think of Hangzhou. Once the news appears in the Shenbao, someone is bound to panic. Who knows what might happen? I must get back. It would be best to reach Hangzhou before the newspaper does.” “Quite right. Last night we discussed only public affairs. I had meant to speak about your household today, but since you have thought of it already, I need say no more. Arrange a boat at once.” “I shall see to it,” Gu said. “As soon as it is ready, I shall return.” After he left, Hu and the Seventh Lady continued their private discussion until noon. Gu then returned to say the boat was arranged. For three hundred taels he had hired a small steamer to tow it; Hu could reach Hangzhou in two days.

Hu had two official boats for his own use, one large and one small. This time he took the smaller, shallow-draught vessel. Towed by the steamer, it travelled as smoothly as a light carriage on a familiar road. At dusk it passed Haining Independent Department and entered Hangzhou prefecture, reaching the provincial capital that night. Hu landed at Wangxian Bridge, hired a small sedan chair, and quietly returned home. “Back so soon?” Madam Luosi asked in surprise. “Did things go smoothly?” “It is too much to explain at once. How is my mother?” “Very well. She is only worrying about you.” Hu sighed softly and fell into a sad silence. “I shall have food prepared. Rest a little first.” Madam Luosi called A’yun. “Tell A’lan to inform Madam that the master has returned.” She was observing the proper distinction between principal wife and concubine, but Hu stopped her. “No, not yet. Let us finish our discussion first.” They talked until the fourth watch before Hu finally went to bed. Madam Luosi did not sleep. She considered matters again and again, then, at the first light of dawn, took A’yun to knock at the door of Mengxiang Tower. After speaking with Mrs Hu for about an hour, she returned, woke Hu, attended to his washing, and had breakfast served—a lavish spread as usual. “From tomorrow, we cannot put on a display like this.” She explained hastily, “It is only because this is your first morning home. The private kitchen wanted to please you.” “The private kitchen can be closed from tomorrow too.” “I understand. I shall arrange these things. You need not trouble yourself about them.”

Hu said no more. Looking over the table, he asked, “Fetch two sticks of ‘fried Hui’ from the main kitchen.” There had been countless treacherous ministers, but Hangzhou people most hated Qin Hui for causing Yue Fei’s death. They therefore called the long fried dough sticks youzha Hui—“deep-fried Hui”—imagining him in an oil cauldron in the eighteenth level of hell. The name was also written youzhuo kuai. With so many servants, the Hu household made its own sesame flatbreads and fried dough every morning in the main kitchen. Hu had never eaten them. His sudden request was merely a declaration that he would live humbly from now on. Madam Luosi thought it too great a humiliation. She also feared the servants would embroider the incident and spread it as news; some might even accuse him of putting on a performance. Without openly objecting, she gave A’yun a look. The clever maid understood, went outside for a while, and returned. “They have put out the fire and stopped frying. Cold dough sticks are dreadful, so I did not bring any.” “Then never mind,” Madam Luosi said. “The master has nearly finished.” Hu said nothing and rose after his porridge. The clock struck eight. He nodded. “It is time.” Madam Luosi began giving orders. “A’yun, have Fusheng and Old Mother He called. Then tell all the concubines to assemble in the second hall. The master has instructions for them. Tell A’lan to ask Madam to come too.” A’yun acknowledged each command. Soon the male and female head servants arrived. Madam Luosi told Fusheng to light a brazier in the hall, then drew Old Mother He aside for a lengthy private briefing.

For the past ten years and more, every night in the Hu household had been like the Lantern Festival, every morning like a holiday. Some concubines were only just getting up and washing; others remained in bed. Two early risers had already heard from their maids that Hu had returned during the night. One, indolent by nature, gave the news no further thought. She cared only about her parrot and bowl of goldfish. The cold had killed two fish, leaving her out of sorts. The other was goodhearted and always tried to please Hu. Knowing that he liked his women carefully adorned, she arranged pearls and jade all over her hair and put on a brand-new fur-lined coat of dark satin. She expected to see him at noon: whenever he returned from a distant journey, he invariably gathered his twelve concubines for a family meal. Times had changed, but she assumed the old custom would remain. Thus, when summoned, she was first to reach the second hall. Hu’s eyes brightened. “Why, dressed like a flower so early! Are you hurrying off to a wedding feast?” Miss Song ranked fifth among the concubines. He had always liked her gentleness and her generous, easygoing nature, which had remained unchanged despite their reverses. That was why he joked with her. Unhurriedly, she first greeted Mrs Hu and Madam Luosi, then answered with a smile, “When I heard you were home, I had to dress properly before seeing you.” “Quite right. The more you wear, the better.” Madam Luosi coughed heavily, as though reproaching him for saying too much. Miss Song could not suspect his hidden meaning. Catching sight of someone, she said, “The Fujian lady is here.” Mistress Yang, the Fujian concubine, wore everyday clothes. Her hair was arranged, but without even a pith flower. She greeted everyone in turn, still thinking about her two dead goldfish and without a smile. The others arrived gradually. At last Madam Luosi said, “Everyone is here.” Hu coughed. The entire place grew so quiet that a dropped needle could have been heard. Yet he could only stare from one woman to another, unable to begin, tears glistening at the corners of his eyes.

No one else knew what he felt, but Mrs Hu and Madam Luosi understood perfectly. He had chosen all eleven women himself, winning some with lavish betrothal gifts and others only after many difficulties. Each had truly been hard to obtain, and each had her own attractions. Whatever reverses he suffered among officials, merchants, or foreigners, at home there was always someone suited to his mood who could help him forget his troubles for a while. How could he harden himself to see these rooms emptied? Madam Luosi acted decisively. “Let Madam speak to everyone.” She was about to tell A’lan, standing behind Mrs Hu, to help him inside. Then she noticed Mistress Zhu, who ranked seventh, and changed her mind. “Little Sister Seven, take the master to the back.” Understanding that there was a purpose behind this, Mistress Zhu came to assist him. He shook his head without a word and turned to go, but she hurried after him and supported his arm.

“The master returned last night,” Mrs Hu began. “The news is very bad. I need not give the details. In a word, when the tree falls, the monkeys scatter. Each of you must make your own arrangements.” A slight commotion passed through the hall. She coughed sharply and waited for silence, but someone spoke before she could continue. It was Mistress Dai, the second concubine. “I am forty this year. I have no family and nowhere to go. I shall stay with you, Madam—rice if there is rice, porridge if there is porridge. I have shared your good fortune; it is only right to share your hardship.” “Mistress Dai, do not say...” Mrs Hu stopped as Madam Luosi tugged at her, then turned to let her speak. The latter saw that persuading Dai would take time; if she refused to be persuaded, everything might come to a standstill. “Explain the arrangement first,” she said quietly. “Ask them one by one. Those who wish to stay can be discussed separately.” Mrs Hu resumed. “The master has no choice. He has been dismissed from office, and we do not know what further charges may follow. Rather than let everyone suffer with him, he must ask you to provide for yourselves. He has managed to assemble some ready silver: five hundred taels apiece for your living expenses. There is no need to return to your rooms. ‘Generals, do not dismount; each ride on towards your own future.’ We must part here.”

Mistress Yang was the first to move. Leaning on a maid’s shoulder, she hurried from the hall to the garden entrance. The gate was shut and secured with a large lock; Old Mother He stood beside it. “Open it! I must get my things.” “You cannot go in, Mistress Yang. I have no key.” “Where is it?” “With the master.” “I do not believe you.” “Then there is nothing I can do. Let it go.” “My parrot and goldfish have not been fed,” Yang said through tears. “Do not worry. Someone will look after them. They will not die.” Yang wanted to argue, but Old Mother He remained silent and stony-faced. Seeing no way around her, she returned miserably to the hall. There everyone was talking at once. Some discussed where to go, some considered in silence, and others reproached themselves: had they known, they would have followed Miss Song’s example and worn all their jewellery. Their expressions varied too. Some wept at the prospect of parting; some looked bewildered, as though their wings had been clipped; others were visibly delighted, ready to fly as soon as the cage opened. The male and female servants gathered outside showed still more complicated feelings. Most stood in little groups whispering. Excitement and slyness on certain faces made their thoughts easy to guess: they hoped to pick up a ready-made advantage. Young, unmarried male servants, in particular, seemed to see a swan descending from the sky straight towards their mouths. A chance to acquire both a woman and her money was beyond their wildest dreams. After a period of confusion, matters were largely settled. Mistress Dai alone insisted on staying and was to go and keep Old Madam Hu company. Five would return to their parents’ homes; four remained undecided, intending either to seek relatives or rent temporary accommodation—nine in all. Mrs Hu instructed the head servants to hire transport and provide escorts for those going to family. Those renting rooms probably had plans of their own and someone to attend to them, so the household need not intervene.

That left only Mistress Zhu, whose arrangements Hu Xueyan was making himself. “Seven,” he said, “you come from a respectable family. That is why I have always treated you with particular consideration. You know that yourself.” “I know,” she answered, lowering her head. “Before I went to Shanghai this time,” he continued, “Sister Luo spoke to you about Zhou Shaotang. What do you think?” “I have never really thought about it. I took it as a joke.” “It was no joke,” Hu said as gently as he could. “I know you do not want to leave, but circumstances give us no choice. As the saying goes, husband and wife are birds of the same wood: when disaster comes, each must fly its own way. You must try to accept it.” “How can I? I have been with you for eight years, wearing silks and satins, with pearls and jade for my jewels. After enjoying such comforts, how can I go and live in someone else’s house?” Her resistance was beginning to soften. Hu saw through her as clearly as though he had swallowed a firefly that lit up his insides. After a moment’s thought, he lowered his voice. “The arrangement I made with my wife and the others is to give each woman five hundred taels, without letting her return to her room. In your case, of course, there will be an exception.” A great weight lifted from her heart. She immediately sank into a graceful bow. “Thank you, Master.” “Get up, get up. How much money have you put aside?” “I have never counted it carefully. Besides, your gifts to me have all been jewelry, and I cannot value them.” “What about silver?” “I have more than twenty thousand taels in the bank.”

All the concubines in the Hu household kept private savings at Fukang to earn interest. When the bank failed, they had hurried to withdraw them, and Hu had instructed that all these deposits were to be paid. He was therefore surprised that Mistress Zhu still had more than twenty thousand taels there. “What? You have not withdrawn your money?” “I did not want to.” “Why?” “With this happening to you, it would have looked far too mercenary if I had gone to withdraw my twenty thousand taels.” “Good! Good! Sister Luo and I have not been wrong to think so highly of you.” He paused, then asked, “Where is your passbook?” “In my room.” “Give it to me later. I shall give you another sum of money.” “Please do not,” she said. “You have more than enough trouble of your own.”

Hu then spoke of Zhou Shaotang: even as a young man he had stood out from the crowd. His ready tongue might make him seem a little slippery, but in practical matters he was thoroughly dependable. Hu went on to describe Mrs Zhou’s good character; if Mistress Zhu married into that household, they could all live together in harmony. She remained silent throughout. Whether she was even listening was doubtful, for she either hung her head or gazed out of the window, apparently absorbed in her own thoughts. This began to worry Hu. “What do you really think?” he asked. “I—I should like to ask my elder brother.” “A father decides a first marriage; a woman decides her own remarriage. Your father is dead. What right has your brother to interfere?” She hesitated without replying. Just then the door opened softly, and Madam Luosi appeared. “Is everything settled?” Hu asked. “Only Mistress Dai absolutely refuses to go. She is willing to serve Old Madam instead.” “Oh.” Hu nodded without committing himself. “And Miss Song?” “She is going back to her parents. She wanted to come in and kowtow to you, but I said seeing you would only make her sad, so there was no need.” “She does have a conscience.” Pointing to Mistress Zhu, he added, “She has more than twenty thousand taels at Fukang. Everyone else withdrew their deposits last month, but she did not.” “Oh,” said Madam Luosi, and went no further.

At that moment someone knocked. It was Fusheng, bringing in a newly delivered copy of the Shenbao. The paper carried news of Hu’s dismissal and of the order placing his case in Zuo Zongtang’s hands. There was also an item under “Local News”: “Previous issues have reported that Mi Benchang, the manager of the Fukang establishment opened by Circuit Intendant Hu Xueyan in Jixian Lane in the British Settlement, went into hiding following a shortage in the accounts, causing the bank to close. We now learn that Mi first returned to his native Ningbo, then went to Hangzhou, where he did not venture to seek an audience with Intendant Hu, and subsequently returned to Shanghai. Intendant Hu arrived here a few days ago and arranged to meet him. Unexpectedly, Mi took poison and died that same night. Only on the morning of the day before yesterday was his suicide discovered. His swollen abdomen and traces of vomited blood suggest that he died after swallowing a Western medicinal fluid.”

How Mi had died no longer mattered to Hu. What concerned him was another article combining anecdote with comment, entitled “The God of Wealth Hu Ruined by Extravagance.” One passage read: “Hu built great residences in both Shanghai and Hangzhou. The Hangzhou mansion was particularly magnificent, following imperial patterns and Western designs, repeatedly demolished and rebuilt. Ancient ritual wine vessels covered the walls of the reception halls, with scarcely an empty space: all were Qin or Han antiquities, each worth a fortune. The walls were coated with finely crushed pottery grit, rough to the touch and capable of lasting a hundred years without decay. In the garden was an Immortals’ Grotto resembling a cellar, its tables and couches arranged in orderly rows. In the sixth and seventh months Hu would lie there wrapped in heavy furs, unaware that anywhere in the world there was such a thing as oppressive summer heat.” At this Hu laughed aloud. Madam Luosi and Mistress Zhu drew close, and he explained the passage to them. “What does ‘heavy furs’ mean?” Madam Luosi asked. “A fur robe?” “Even if not a fur robe, it would mean at least a lined jacket. It is certainly cooler inside the rockery, but how could anyone need a lined jacket there in the sixth or seventh month? Let me see who is talking such nonsense.” Looking more carefully, he found that the article appeared under the general heading “Nanting Notes,” and that its author was Li Boyuan.

Another passage read: “Once, in shabby clothes, Hu visited a courtesan, who treated him with contempt and offered no courtesies. An old woman, however, inquired after him attentively. Touched by her sincerity, he sat for a while before leaving. The next day he sent the old woman a small packet. When she opened it, gleaming gold leaf lay within. Deeply regretting her conduct, the courtesan sent the old woman to his door to ask him to visit again. Hu said nothing, merely stroking his beard and smiling. On another occasion he passed a tailor’s shop, where a slender young woman stood in the doorway. He stared at her; noticing him, she went inside and shut the door. Angered, Hu sent someone to her father to propose taking her as a concubine. Her father held out and would not consent. Hu offered seven thousand dollars, and an agreement was reached. On the chosen day he entertained guests, then entered the bridal chamber and continued drinking alone. When drunk, he ordered the woman to lie naked on the bed. A great candle was held beside her while he walked around examining her. Throwing back his beard, he laughed aloud: ‘The other day you would not let me look at you. What can you do now?’” Hu laughed again. “Listen to this Li Boyuan! He gives me a great big beard.” He read and explained the passage to the two women. “Malicious gossip!” Madam Luosi exclaimed. “Nothing of the sort ever happened!” “And he contradicts himself,” said Mistress Zhu, who, as a doctor’s daughter, had some literary education. “First it is ‘stroking his beard and smiling,’ then ‘throwing back his beard and laughing aloud.’ He invents so many rumors that he loses track of them himself.” “Quite right. But the next passage is rather interesting. It is almost as though he knew things would end as they have today.” “Oh? What does he say?” Madam Luosi asked. “He says: ‘Shortly afterward, Hu hurried away to sleep elsewhere. At dawn he sent an old woman to tell her: Take everything in this room and marry someone else; there is no place for you here. She did as instructed and took property worth more than twenty thousand taels back to her father, making him immensely rich.’”

“This man has a very narrow idea of the world,” Mistress Zhu said. “Does having twenty thousand taels make someone immensely rich?” Hu said nothing. “How much would you say it takes?” Madam Luosi asked. Turning her own words over in her mind, Mistress Zhu realized that her unguarded remark had aroused suspicion. After a moment she answered, “I was laughing at this Mr Li for having an even narrower outlook than mine. He thinks twenty thousand taels an enormous amount. I have more than twenty thousand taels myself, and I am willing to give it up.” She meant her deposit at Fukang, once again declaring that she would forgo it. She was free, of course, to make generous speeches. Hu saw no need to argue seriously with her; he had only to proceed as he intended. Madam Luosi felt it still less appropriate to say anything more. But Mistress Zhu’s lack of desire to fight for a larger share of the property was now plain to see, and Madam Luosi liked her the better for it.

The hall had fallen quiet, but Madam Luosi and Mrs Hu still had to arrange the dismissal of the male and female servants according to their plan, so Mistress Zhu continued to keep Hu company. “Let us go inside,” he said. “It is too cold here.” “They cannot open the garden gate yet. Sit a little longer, Master. I shall have another brazier brought.” She was away a long time, and nobody came to attend to him. When he wanted tea, it was cold; when he searched the drawers for a book, he found only an almanac. A saying came to mind: “Reading the almanac on New Year’s Eve—all the good days are over.” Mistress Zhu eventually returned. As soon as the eleven concubines had answered the summons to the second hall, Old Mother He and A’yun had locked a number of doors and assembled the maids and serving women in the servants’ quarters to await instructions. Mistress Zhu had first found her senior maid Chunxiang among them, then sent her searching everywhere. Only after considerable difficulty had Chunxiang found a basket of charcoal, which accounted for the long delay. Fresh charcoal was added to the brazier, and water was boiled in a copper kettle over it. With hot tea and warmth restored, Hu suddenly heard his stomach rumble. “Where are we eating?” “It will have to be here.” Mistress Zhu told Chunxiang, “Tell the private kitchen to serve the Master’s meal here.” “It is no use my telling them. Under the rules, the private kitchen only takes orders from Madam Luosi’s people.” “Then find A’yun.” Chunxiang went and soon returned. “A’yun and I went together. Mother Liu says the private kitchen is not cooking today. She did not even know the Master was back, so nothing has been prepared. But having nothing else to do, she has cooked tomorrow’s Laba porridge. She asks whether the Master would like some.”

“Why is the private kitchen not cooking today?” Hu asked. “That must have been Madam Luosi’s instruction,” Mistress Zhu answered. He understood: cutting off the food was another expedient she had been driven to adopt, since it would force everyone to leave at once. He strongly disapproved and shook his head. “This goes too far. Suppose someone says after leaving, ‘I went out through the Hu family gates on an empty stomach!’ Think how that would sound.” “It cannot be helped. Please do not blame Madam Luosi.” “I do not blame her. I blame myself. I should have thought of it.” Mistress Zhu fell silent. When Mother Liu arrived with helpers to serve the meal, she actually managed to produce four plates and four bowls, though everything had been thrown together from ingredients at hand. There was even an assorted hotpot. At the turn of the year, great old households enjoyed a succession of seasonal delicacies. The Hu family, accustomed to lavish dining, took particular care over the porridge served on the eighth day of the twelfth month, since Old Madam Hu was a Buddhist. It came in three grades. The main kitchen prepared the middle and lowest grades for employees and servants. The best was specially made in the private kitchen, and apart from the family’s superiors, only guests and a few senior employees were allowed it. The sweet version contained pine nuts, lotus seeds, dried longan, red dates, and other dried fruits; the savory version had fine mushrooms, dried bamboo shoots, and other delicacies. Medicinal ingredients reputed to nourish and strengthen the body were added as well. Today, with the beautiful concubines scattered like clouds and decline visible everywhere, only these two kinds of Laba porridge remained as they had always been. The thought stirred Hu’s sorrow, but also comforted him. “I shall have both sweet and savory,” he said with pleasure. “Savory first, sweet afterward,” Mistress Zhu advised. “If you eat the sweet first, the savory will have no taste.” “Quite right,” he replied. “Let the sweetness come afterward.”

The porridge was served. Hu had just picked up his chopsticks when something occurred to him, and he immediately put them down again. “What is it?” “Has any been sent to Old Madam?” “I do not know.” Mistress Zhu hastily called, “Mother Liu! Mother Liu!” Mother Liu, waiting outside, came in at once. At the question she stood bewildered. “Madam Luosi gave no instructions,” she stammered. Hu had not once lost his temper since Fukang’s troubles began. Now he could no longer restrain himself. He brought his hand down on the table. “No instructions, so you do nothing!” he roared. “Have you forgotten how well Old Madam has always treated you? Because she is away, you cannot even remember her! Such ingratitude—you are scarcely human!” Nobody in the room had ever seen him so angry. Mistress Zhu promptly knelt, and the others naturally followed her example. “Please do not be angry, Master. Today is the seventh.” “Today is the seventh, so is tomorrow not the eighth? How long do you think you can put it off?” Unjustly scolded, she felt hurt, but dared neither defend herself nor cry. She answered briefly, “It will be sent up the hill at once. I shall take it myself.” Only then did his anger abate, though grief remained. In former years, had they not always made a trial batch on the seventh and sought Old Madam’s approval before preparing the proper batch? Now nobody even cared where she was. How could her son’s heart not feel as though a knife were cutting through it?

Meanwhile Madam Luosi had been told that the Master was furious because no Laba porridge had been sent to Old Madam. Knowing she had been careless, she hurried over to deal with it. By the time she arrived, the storm had passed, but she could imagine that Hu’s anger had not wholly subsided. Fortunately Mother Liu had received many favors from her; she could be made to endure a little injustice to draw off his remaining anger. Madam Luosi therefore confronted her sternly. “Today is the seventh, not the day for Laba porridge. Why did you serve it?” “I asked A’lan whether the Master would like a bowl, since it was ready,” Mother Liu faltered. “I did not bring it on my own initiative.” “Still arguing!” Madam Luosi shouted. “Once you have cooked it, naturally it must be eaten. Otherwise are we to throw it away? Every year the porridge goes into the pot only when the zi hour begins, around midnight. Why did you cook it so early?” “Because there was to be no cooking today—” “Who told you that?” Madam Luosi cut in. “Was the Master to go without food? What did I tell you? I said there would be business and confusion today, and the Master might not be able to eat in peace, so the meal should be served later. When did I ever say there would be no cooking?” Her voice rose as though she were truly furious. Mother Liu dared not answer. Hu was beginning to feel uncomfortable and was about to intervene, but Madam Luosi only grew more vehement.

“And you know our old custom perfectly well: Old Madam always tastes the trial porridge before the main batch is cooked. This year she is staying on the hill. I had not decided whether to send it up or take the ingredients there and cook it on the spot. Yet you went ahead and cooked it before the proper time!” She struck the table hard. “How dare you!” By now Hu’s anger had entirely vanished. Feeling deeply guilty, he regretted making so much of a small matter and began soothing Madam Luosi and comforting Mother Liu. “Enough, enough! There is no need to be so angry. It is all my fault.” To Mother Liu he added, “You have done nothing wrong. Do not take Madam Luosi’s scolding to heart.” “I would not dare.” Mistress Zhu and A’lan also helped make peace, one pouring tea and the other wringing out a towel to attend to Madam Luosi. In an instant the storm dissolved.

“The porridge is not bad,” Hu said. “Have a bowl yourself.” “I am not hungry,” Madam Luosi replied, her expression quite composed. “Once I have finished making the arrangements, I shall go with Madam to see Old Madam.” “Are you both going?” “Of course. Surely she must be told about such a great change in the family? Once Mistress Dai arrives, she will find out anyway and begin to worry.” This reminded Hu how momentous the upheaval was. By the rules of the family, he ought to have sought his mother’s instructions before acting. If she thought he had taken too much upon himself and felt hurt, how could he be at peace? “I shall go too,” he said. “How can you? If urgent news comes, there will be nobody to decide what to do. With everyone up on the hill, they will not know where to reach us.” “True enough. But I am afraid she will blame me for not saying a word to her about something so important.” “Do not worry. I know what to say.” “What will you tell her?” Mistress Zhu was out of sight, and only A’lan remained, but Madam Luosi did not want even her to hear. “Where is Mother Liu?” “Back in the private kitchen.” “Ask her to come.” “Yes.” Only when A’lan was well away did Madam Luosi speak. “I shall tell Old Madam that if we had asked her beforehand, her kind heart would never have allowed it, and nothing could have been done. It was better to say nothing and let Madam and me be the villains.” She added, “What I do not know is whether to tell her that you have lost your official position.” The subject saddened Hu. “What do you think?” Madam Luosi devised a compromise: she would say he had resigned, without mentioning dismissal. He acquiesced without enthusiasm.

A’yun now came quietly up and whispered, “Nearly finished.” “Oh? Where is Madam?” Madam Luosi asked. “Her liver-qi trouble has come on again. She has gone upstairs.” “Is it serious?” “No. Madam says she is simply too tired and will be better after a rest. Shall we fetch her when it is time to open the rooms?” “Has everyone left?” By “everyone,” Madam Luosi meant the dismissed servants. There were so many of them: some were collecting their extra three months’ wages from the accounts office, others were packing, and others still had to hand over their duties to those who would remain. It would be evening before they had all dispersed. This did not, however, prevent the rooms from being opened, since the garden formed a separate domain. After thinking for a moment, Madam Luosi discovered a difficulty. “Has anyone learned the coppersmith’s trade?” she asked with a frown. Hu, who had been silent, looked surprised. “What do you need a coppersmith for?” “To open the locks.” He said no more. A’yun understood too. “Guixing, who does odd jobs in the gatehouse, used to be apprenticed to a coppersmith. But he is leaving as well. Shall I see whether he is still here and keep him back?” “Not if he is leaving.” “Then shall we call in a coppersmith?” “Still less suitable.” Madam Luosi thought, then said decisively, “Tell Fusheng to get axes and hammers. What does it matter if a few chests are broken?” That morning, as soon as the concubines and their maids had left the garden, their rooms had been locked. There were keys to the room doors, but none for the locked chests inside, which was why a coppersmith was needed. Yet word that they were forcibly seizing the private savings of discarded concubines would sound very ugly. After weighing it repeatedly, Madam Luosi decided to sacrifice the chests instead.

“Master,” Madam Luosi said, “you can go inside now.” The rooms stood empty of their occupants, and their chests were about to be broken open in a search for valuables. It was too painful. Hu shook his head. “I should like to go out for a walk.” “Where do you mean to go? Why not visit Treasurer De?” By rights he should already have called on Dexin. But such a visit would mean discussing business, and he was so exhausted in mind and spirit that he shrank from serious subjects. He merely shook his head. “Or perhaps visit your new relation by marriage?” She meant Philanthropist Wang. Hu reflected that the visit would involve endless courtesies, and all that ceremony was more than he could bear. “I cannot face social calls,” he said. “I should like somewhere quiet where I can listen to people telling jokes.” “Then you can only go to Zhou Shaotang.” “Yes!” Hu rose at once. “I shall go and see Shaotang.” “Wait!” Madam Luosi said hastily. “Let us talk first.”
